newsitem.title: UK: Pressure mounts on British MP to step down.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on British MP to step down.

text.p: Morality in politics dominated the British election campaign on Friday with the ruling Conservatives persistently dogged by sleaze and sex allegations.

Pressure mounted on Conservative member of parliament Piers Merchant to step down before the May 1 election. He has denied newspaper allegations that he had an affair with a 17-year-old nightclub hostess.
Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney, calling the reports a distraction, said he hoped Merchant's local constituency would speedily decide on the lawmaker's future.

"I hope that meeting is called quickly and that we can move onto the substantive issues which will determine the outcome of this election campaign," he told BBC Radio after two bruising weeks for the party which has been in power for the past 18 years.

The Conservatives, buoyed by low inflation, falling unemployment and a strong economy, had hoped to concentrate their fire on the links between the opposition Labour Party, strong favourite to win the election, and Britain's trade unions. But sleaze is dominating the headlines.
On Wednesday, former junior minister Tim Smith stood down as a candidate over his failure to declare that he had accepted cash in return for asking questions of ministers in parliament.
Then the tabloid Sun newspaper, which had declared its support for Labour, printed a series of photographs showing the married Merchant kissing blonde teenager Anna Cox.
Merchant denied the story, saying: "Anna is a dear friend of mine and has been helping with my campaign. But there is no question of us having an affair. I have never made love to her."
Rod Reed, party chief in Merchant's southern England constituency of Beckenham -- traditionally a Conservative stronghold, has summoned him for questioning on Tuesday after the Easter weekend break.
"I think we have to be fair to the man and hear his side of the story," he said.
"It's in the interests of natural justice. We can't hang someone out to dry just on the basis of three or four pages of tittle-tattle in the Sun," he told BBC Radio.
To add to the woes of the beleaguered Conservatives, former government minister Allan Stewart was taken to hospital on Thursday suffering from a nervous breakdown, party officials said.
He had agreed to step down as a parliamentary candidate on Tuesday after press reports linked him to a married woman he is said to have met while attending a clinic specialising in alcohol problems.

But the latest opinion poll did offer some comfort to the Conservatives who under Prime Minister John Major are bidding to win their fifth election victory in a row. The Harris poll for the Independent newspaper showed that Labour's huge lead had fallen by three points.
But the Conservatives were still 24 points behind Labour, revived by the centrist Tony Blair who has ditched much of the party's socialist dogma.

Plans for a televised debate between Britain's top two political leaders collapsed on Thursday night with Labour's campaign manager Peter Mandelson accusing the Conservatives of being "unable to be flexible and to come to a final decision".
That provoked an angry retort on Friday from Conservative party chairman Mawhinney who said: "Mr Blair is terrified, he's chicken."
